h1:
Phetchaburi Thai Desserts
The Famous Shops Below Khao Wang
intro: Phetchaburi is known as the capital of Thai desserts, mostly because fresh palm sugar from the toddy palms ringing the town is the main ingredient. That gives Phetchaburi sweets a fragrance and a soft, mellow sweetness you really can taste against versions from elsewhere. Most of the famous shops are clustered below Khao Wang (Phra Nakhon Khiri) — mor kaeng custard, thong yip, thong yot, foi thong, right down to sticky-rice slices. We've picked the shops that locals actually buy from and that reviews keep mentioning, and ranked them for you.
chips: 🟡 Thong yip · thong yot · foi thong

blocks.html: If you drive through Phetchaburi and don't stop for sweets, you're missing the town's signature treat. The single biggest cluster of famous dessert shops is below Khao Wang, along Khiri Ratthaya Road and Ratchawithi Road — walk a few steps and you'll pass a dozen shops in a row. Many have been making and selling for 40–60 years. What ties Phetchaburi sweets together is real palm sugar, fresh duck eggs and home-pressed coconut milk, which give a soft, fragrant, rich sweetness rather than the sharp edge you get from white sugar.

items: Fresh palm sugar — the heart of Phetchaburi sweets, simmered down from the flower stalks of toddy palms around town, with a distinctive fragrance and a softer sweetness than white sugar.
Fresh duck eggs — thong yip, thong yot and foi thong here are usually made with duck eggs, which give a deeper yellow and a denser texture.
Mor kaeng topped with fried shallots — Phetchaburi's signature touch is a sprinkle of crisp fried shallots on top of the custard, cutting the sweetness with a savory aroma.
Made fresh daily — most of the famous shops bake and fry a new batch every morning, and they sell out fast on long holiday weekends.

blocks.html: This ranking is drawn from real reviews and from how popular each shop is among locals and the people who drive through. It isn't a fixed ladder of which shop is strictly better, because each one is strong on a different sweet — the honest advice is to try a few and compare which suits your taste. Prices are rough ranges for 2025–2026 and may shift with ingredient costs.

items.name: Mae Kim Lai (Rai Som)
items.blurb: One of the legendary mor kaeng names in Phetchaburi, and the one drivers stop for as a souvenir more than any other. Made with fresh duck eggs, freshly pressed coconut milk and shallots fried in-house every day, with several fillings to choose from — taro, mung bean, pumpkin and lotus seed. Several branches around the bypass and Tha Yang, so it's easy to find.
items.meta: Souvenir/mor kaeng · several branches (Rai Som–Tha Yang–bypass)

items.name: Mae Kim Lang
items.blurb: Another famous shop from Phetchaburi's family of "Mae" makers, strong on mor kaeng topped with crisp, fragrant fried shallots over a smooth, fine-textured custard. Has egg, taro and mung-bean mor kaeng plus the gold-sweet set. The shop is in town, and it's one locals buy from to eat at home.
items.meta: Mor kaeng/Thai sweets · in Phetchaburi town

items.name: Mae Bun Lon
items.blurb: A long-running shop that leans on freshly pressed coconut milk and fresh duck eggs every day. The mor kaeng is well-rounded in an old-fashioned way and not too sweet — many people get hooked on how rich its coconut milk is.

items.name: Mae Bun Lom
items.blurb: An old recipe carried on for more than 60 years, with a soft sweetness and the fragrance of palm sugar. Regulars order from here for years, and it works both for eating yourself and buying as a gift.

items.name: Mae Lamiad
items.blurb: Known for one of the most fragrant coconut milk aromas in town. The mor kaeng is dense with a crisp fried-shallot top, and reviewers often mention how rich and fragrant it is — good for anyone who likes a deeply flavored mor kaeng.

items.name: Lung Anek Phetchaburi Sweets
items.blurb: A shop that makes many kinds of Phetchaburi sweets in one place — mor kaeng, foi thong, thong yip, thong yot and met khanun. Prices are friendly, so it's a good stop to put together a mixed souvenir set all at once.

items.name: Sa-nguan Pho Phra
items.blurb: An old shop that stakes its name on real ingredients with no added flavor or color. The mor kaeng and Thai sweets taste natural — a good fit for anyone who wants the genuine traditional flavor without artificial sweetness.

items.name: Waraporn Fresh Foi Thong
items.blurb: If foi thong is your main target, this shop stands out for fresh foi thong with fine, neatly arranged strands and a soft sweetness from palm sugar. It also has thong yip, thong yot and met khanun for the full gold-sweet set — good for merit-making and auspicious gifts.

items.name: Mae Pin
items.blurb: A genuine old-recipe shop in town, with well-rounded mor kaeng and Thai sweets that locals stop for regularly. The shop isn't big, but everything is made fresh daily.

items.name: Phet Suphaphan
items.blurb: Strong on mor kaeng baked fresh every day, with a pretty top and a smooth texture. It's easy to find along the souvenir strip — a good quick stop on the way up to or down from Bangkok.

items.name: Khanom Nok Noi (Mae Lai)
items.blurb: A Thai-sweets shop with more than 50 kinds in one place — khanom chan, khanom piakpoon, sticky-rice slices and coconut-milk sweets. Good for anyone who wants to taste a range of Thai sweets in one set.

items.name: Khao Wang Dessert Market (Combined Stalls)
items.blurb: If you don't want to commit to one shop, just walk the dessert market below Khao Wang. There are rows of stalls from several makers, so you can taste and compare in one spot — sticky-rice slices, khanom tan, mor kaeng and the gold-sweet set. You can haggle a little if you buy several boxes.

blocks.title: Tips to buy smart
blocks.html: Mor kaeng and the gold-sweet set are made fresh daily, and they often sell out by early afternoon on long holiday weekends. If you want a fresh batch, stop by mid-morning to noon, and pick a tray where the fried-shallot top is still crisp, not soggy.

blocks.text: Phetchaburi sweets you have to try

items: Mor kaeng (baked custard) — the town's star, a custard of egg, taro or mung bean baked until the top browns and topped with fried shallots, sweet and rich with the aroma of palm sugar.
Thong yip — pleated sheets of egg yolk shaped into flower petals, soft and sweet with a golden color from duck eggs, popular at auspicious events.
Thong yot — drops of egg yolk in round beads, glazed in fragrant syrup, sweet and juicy in just the right amount.
Foi thong — fine threads of egg yolk arranged in folds, soft and sweet, and a great match with black coffee.
Sticky-rice slices (khao niao tat) — coconut sticky rice cut into pieces, topped with sangkhaya custard or beans, a local snack that's easy to find below Khao Wang.
Khanom tan (toddy palm cake) — made with ripe toddy-palm flesh, fragrant and softly sweet — a sweet that really shows off Phetchaburi's palm-town roots.

blocks.text: A walking route for dessert shopping near Khao Wang

blocks.html: If you're already visiting Phra Nakhon Khiri (Khao Wang), half a day is just right to add on a dessert-shopping walk. Here's an easy order to do it in.

blocks.label: Half day
blocks.title: Walk, eat and shop for sweets below Khao Wang

items.activity: Go up Phra Nakhon Khiri (Khao Wang)
items.note: Take the tram or walk up to see the palace on the hill and the view over Phetchaburi, then come back down to find food.

items.activity: Stop at the dessert market below Khao Wang
items.note: Walk the rows of dessert stalls from several makers, sample sticky-rice slices and khanom tan before you buy.

items.activity: Buy mor kaeng from 1–2 famous shops
items.note: Pick Mae Kim Lai / Mae Kim Lang / Mae Lamiad, compare the flavors, and choose a tray where the fried-shallot top is still crisp.

items.activity: Grab a gold-sweet set as a gift
items.note: Thong yip, thong yot and foi thong from Waraporn or Lung Anek, boxed up as an auspicious set.
Find a cafe in the old town and sip black coffee with foi thong — it cuts the sweetness just right.

blocks.title: Packing for a long drive
blocks.html: Mor kaeng keeps about 2–3 days in the fridge, but thong yip, thong yot and foi thong last longer. If you're driving a long way back to Bangkok, set the mor kaeng aside to eat first and save the gold-sweet set for the people back home.

faq.q: Where are Phetchaburi's famous dessert shops?
faq.a: Most are clustered below Khao Wang (Phra Nakhon Khiri), along Khiri Ratthaya and Ratchawithi roads, with shops lined up one after another. Famous mor kaeng makers like Mae Kim Lai also have branches around the bypass and Tha Yang, so they're convenient to stop at when driving through.

faq.q: Which Phetchaburi mor kaeng is the best?
faq.a: The names people mention most often are Mae Kim Lai, Mae Kim Lang, Mae Bun Lon, Mae Bun Lom and Mae Lamiad. Each is strong in a different way — some have a crisp fried-shallot top, others a very fragrant coconut milk — so the honest advice is to try a few and compare which suits your taste.

faq.q: How much does Phetchaburi mor kaeng cost?
faq.a: Through 2025–2026, prices run around 50–60 THB for a small tray, depending on the filling and size. Gold sweets like thong yip, thong yot and foi thong start at around 40–80 THB per box or per 100g.

faq.q: Why do Phetchaburi sweets taste sweeter and more fragrant than elsewhere?
faq.a: Because they use fresh palm sugar from the toddy palms around town as the main ingredient, which gives a distinctive fragrance and a softer sweetness than white sugar. Add fresh duck eggs and home-pressed coconut milk, and the flavor comes out well-rounded in the original style.

faq.q: How long do Phetchaburi sweets keep?
faq.a: Mor kaeng keeps about 2–3 days in the fridge and is best eaten first. Thong yip, thong yot and foi thong last a little longer, which makes them well suited as gifts to take home.
